title: Naan-e taftoon
subtitle: Thin Persian flatbread with sesame seeds
excerpt: Naan-e taftoon is a thin, slightly blistered Persian flatbread made with plain flour and a little yoghurt for softness. It bakes in four minutes on a very hot pan or griddle. Eaten hot from the pan with white cheese and herbs for breakfast, or as a wrap for kebabs.
sourceNotes: Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Taftoon documented as one of the four main Persian breads alongside barbari, lavash, and sangak. Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Notes on the slightly leavened, thin character of taftoon.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked flatbreads. Reheat directly in a dry pan for one minute per side.
recipe.batchNotes: The dough keeps in the fridge for up to two days. Roll and cook fresh to order.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can rest overnight in the fridge. Shape and cook fresh on the day.
recipe.temperatureNote: Cook on the highest heat your hob can produce. The pan must be smoking hot.

content.text: Naan-e taftoon is a thin, slightly leavened Persian flatbread cooked on a hot pan rather than in the oven. It blisters where it touches the heat and has a soft, pliable texture that makes it good for wrapping as well as for tearing. The dough includes a little yoghurt, which keeps the crumb tender and adds a slight tang. It comes together in minutes and is best eaten hot from the pan.

Mix {{yeast-dried}} and {{caster-sugar}} into 140 ml of warm water. Leave five minutes until foamy. Combine {{plain-flour}} and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Add the yeast liquid, {{plain-yoghurt}}, and {{olive-oil}}. Mix to a smooth dough and knead for five minutes. It should be soft but not sticky.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 30 minutes to rise slightly. It will not double but should feel puffy and soft.
Heat a heavy frying pan or griddle over the highest heat for at least three minutes until very hot.

Divide the dough into four pieces. Roll each one on a lightly floured surface to a thin circle or oval, about 25 cm across and 2 to 3 mm thick. If using {{sesame-seeds}}, press them lightly into the surface with the rolling pin.

Place the flatbread in the dry pan, seed side up. Cook for two minutes until the underside has charred spots and the bread is starting to puff and blister. Flip and cook for another two minutes. Remove and wrap in a clean cloth to keep soft. Repeat with the remaining dough.

items.symptom: The flatbread is stiff rather than soft
items.cause: Dough too dry or cooked for too long
items.fix: Wrap each flatbread in a cloth immediately after cooking: the steam keeps it soft. The yoghurt in the dough should also keep it pliable.
The pan must be smoking before the bread goes in. Hold your hand 10 cm above it: you should feel strong heat immediately.

items.symptom: The bread sticks to the pan
items.cause: Pan not dry or dough too sticky
items.fix: Use a completely dry pan with no oil. Lightly flour the bread surface before cooking if it feels sticky.
Roll to 2 to 3 mm: it will puff during cooking. A thicker bread won't cook through properly on a hot pan.

content.text: Taftoon is one of the four classic Iranian breads, the others being barbari, lavash, and sangak. Each has a distinct character: taftoon is thin, slightly leavened, and cooked on a domed clay plate or a hot pan; it sits between the crispy cracker-like lavash and the thick, glossy barbari. It is eaten for breakfast with white cheese, fresh herbs, and walnuts, or served alongside a main meal. In Iran it is made by specialist noonvayi shops and sold fresh and hot, though home versions cooked on a flat griddle are also common.
